passage:
"Sahil, why is your umbrella upside down?" giggled Rehana as the monsoon rain drummed on the verandah roof.
"It's a boat! For the frog."
"Frogs don't need boats. They swim!"
"This frog is lazy." Sahil puffed out his cheeks. "Ribbit-ribbit-plop!"
Rehana snorted. "Say it faster!"
"Ribbitribbitplop!"
"Your face looks like a squashed tomato!"
"Then you're a banana in gumboots!"
Rehana laughed so hard she slid off the step. Their Ammi called from inside, "What's so funny?"
"Banana in gumboots!" they both shouted.

qa.q: What did Sahil say his upside-down umbrella was?
qa.a: He said it was a boat for the frog.

qa.q: Why did Rehana laugh so hard she slid off the step?
qa.a: She was delighted and amused by the silly picture of a banana in gumboots. 😄

qa.q: How could Ammi join in their fun?
qa.a: She could ask them to invent another silly animal in rain boots, or add a silly rhyme of her own.

qa.q: What might Ammi think when she hears "Banana in gumboots!"?
qa.a: Ammi might be puzzled at first, then amused, glad the children are enjoying each other on a rainy day.

grounding: Shows young siblings enjoying silly sounds and absurd images during monsoon rain.

passage: It was wedding season in Delhi, and the hall was crowded and loud. Mummy knelt beside Abhinav. "If you stay in your chair during the pheras, you'll get ice cream after." Abhinav sat very straight. When his cousin Gautam ran past waving a balloon, Abhinav gripped the chair. "I can't. Ice cream," he whispered. Later, when Mummy went to get plates, Abhinav hopped off and chased Gautam round a pillar. Seeing her coming back, he raced to his seat. "I sat the whole time!"

qa.q: What did Mummy promise Abhinav?
qa.a: She said he'd get ice cream after if he stayed in his chair during the pheras.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav race back to his seat when Mummy returned?
qa.a: He was worried about losing the ice cream, so he wanted her to see him sitting.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Abhinav understand the rule beyond the reward?
qa.a: She could explain simply why sitting matters during the pheras, such as letting everyone see and hear, and praise him when he remembers without a treat.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel if she found out Abhinav ran off?
qa.a: Mummy might feel a little disappointed, seeing that the ice cream only kept him seated while she watched.

grounding: Illustrates a young child following a rule mainly to earn a treat, and only while he is being watched.

passage: On the last day before the Christmas break, the kindergarten in Shillong had a party. Each child got one star cookie. Neelam had been in the washroom and came back to an empty plate. Her lip trembled. Gargi looked at her own cookie, the last iced star she'd been saving. She broke it in half, slowly, and held out the bigger piece. "You can have this one." Then she looked at her small half and sighed. Teacher Iba smiled. "That was generous, Gargi."

qa.q: What kind of cookie did each child get?
qa.a: Each child got one star cookie.

qa.q: Why did Gargi sigh at her small half?
qa.a: She felt a little sorry to lose part of her treat, even though she chose to share; she felt both kind and disappointed.

qa.q: How could Teacher Iba make sure no child misses out next time?
qa.a: She could keep treats aside for anyone out of the room, while still noticing kind acts like Gargi's.

qa.q: What is it like for Neelam to receive the bigger piece?
qa.a: Neelam probably feels relieved and grateful, and cared for by Gargi. 😊

grounding: Shows a young child sharing a scarce party treat even though it costs her some of her own pleasure.

passage: I'm Jomon, Farida's neighbour. During Ramzan I often go over at sunset. Yesterday her Nani put out jalebis and told Farida, "One now, or three after we break the fast." Farida stared at the plate. Then she sat on her hands, turned her back to it and started singing loudly. Her cousin Sameer ate one and waved it at her. She shut her eyes. When the call to prayer sounded and everyone broke the fast, she got her three. I don't know how she did it; I'd have grabbed one.

qa.q: What did Nani offer Farida?
qa.a: One jalebi now, or three after they break the fast.

qa.q: Why did Farida sit on her hands and turn her back to the plate?
qa.a: She was tempted by the jalebis but wanted the three later, so she felt determined to keep herself from grabbing one.

qa.q: How could Farida's family encourage this waiting in other situations?
qa.a: They could keep promises as Nani did, so Farida trusts that waiting really brings the bigger reward.

qa.q: How does Jomon see Farida's waiting?
qa.a: Jomon is impressed, admitting that grabbing one would have been hard to resist.

grounding: Illustrates a young child resisting a sweet now so she can have more later, seen by a neighbour.

passage: It was the first rainy week of the new term at a school in Hyderabad. Every time Miss Rukhsana asked a question, Jatin shouted the answer before anyone else could. "Seven! Blue! Elephant!" Asif, beside him, kept his hand up and sighed. On Thursday Miss Rukhsana gave each child a paper leaf. "Hold up your leaf when you know." Jatin's leaf shot up. He bounced in his seat, lips pressed shut. "Jatin?" "Monsoon!" he said, and beamed. Asif got the next turn and grinned at him.

qa.q: What did Miss Rukhsana give each child on Thursday?
qa.a: She gave each child a paper leaf.

qa.q: What does Jatin bouncing with his lips pressed shut suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was excited and eager to answer but trying hard to wait for his turn.

qa.q: What worked in Miss Rukhsana's approach, and why?
qa.a: The paper leaf gave Jatin something to do with his eagerness, so he could wait and still show he knew.

qa.q: What is it like for Asif when Jatin keeps shouting answers?
qa.a: Asif feels frustrated and left out, since a raised hand never gets a turn.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to wait his turn to answer in class instead of shouting out.

passage: I'm Nitin, Jeevan's anna. On Pongal morning our old neighbour, Subramani Thatha, came over with sugarcane. Last year Jeevan hid behind the door. This time he put his palms together and said, "Vanakkam, Thatha," in his soft voice. When Thatha told a long story about his village, Jeevan sat on the mat and didn't interrupt once, though his foot kept jiggling. Thatha patted his head and said he'd grown polite. Jeevan looked at me, eyebrows up, as if he'd won something.

qa.q: What did Subramani Thatha bring on Pongal morning?
qa.a: He came over with sugarcane.

qa.q: What does Jeevan's jiggling foot suggest while he listened?
qa.a: It suggests he felt restless during the long story but chose to stay quiet out of respect.

qa.q: How could the family encourage Jeevan's respectful habits?
qa.a: They could notice his greeting and listening afterwards, and let him offer Thatha water or a sweet next time.

qa.q: How might Subramani Thatha feel about Jeevan's greeting?
qa.a: Thatha seems pleased and warmly touched, noticing Jeevan has grown polite since last year.

grounding: Illustrates a young child greeting an elder respectfully and listening without interrupting during a festival visit.

passage: The week before Eid in Amman, everyone in Siddiq's flat was cleaning. Siddiq's job was to match the shoes by the door and wipe the low windowsill. He did it slowly, tongue between his teeth. His sister Nour swept, and when he tipped the dustpan too early she groaned, "Siddiq!" He scooped the dust back up himself. At school the next day, he noticed the class glue sticks lying uncapped. He capped each one and put them back in the tray before anyone asked.

qa.q: What was Siddiq's job at home?
qa.a: To match the shoes by the door and wipe the low windowsill.

qa.q: How did Siddiq feel when Nour groaned at him?
qa.a: He probably felt a little embarrassed but responsible, so he scooped the dust back up himself.

qa.q: How could Siddiq's teacher encourage his care for class things?
qa.a: The teacher could thank him quietly and give him a small class job, like checking the glue tray each day.

qa.q: How does Nour see Siddiq's help?
qa.a: Nour is irritated by the spilled dust at first, but may appreciate that Siddiq fixes his own mistake.

grounding: Shows a young child doing small chores before a festival and looking after shared classroom things.

passage:
Before the Dussehra holidays: Rukmini sounded out "r-a-m" in her reader, slowly, then guessed "rain". Her cousin Swati giggled, and Rukmini slammed the book shut.
Fourth day of the holidays: Swati sat beside her on the terrace with a torch and a pile of comics while garba music played downstairs. Rukmini traced each word with her finger. "The... man... ran... to... the... fair." She read it twice, faster the second time.
First day back at school: The teacher asked Rukmini to read aloud. She read a whole page, then answered, "He ran because he was late for the fair." Swati, in the next row, gave her a thumbs-up.

qa.q: What did Rukmini first guess instead of "ram"?
qa.a: She guessed "rain".

qa.q: Why did Rukmini slam the book shut before the holidays?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and frustrated when Swati giggled at her mistake.

qa.q: What helped Rukmini's reading improve over the holidays?
qa.a: Reading comics beside a friendly cousin, tracing words with her finger and rereading the same line helped her gain speed and confidence.

qa.q: How does Swati's reaction change from before the holidays to the first day back?
qa.a: Swati first giggles, which stings Rukmini, but later reads beside her and cheers her on with a thumbs-up.

grounding: Illustrates a child moving from slow sound-by-sound decoding to fluent reading with understanding over a festival break.

passage:
"Damini, there are twelve kaju barfis and four of us. How many does each get?" Tarun asked, holding the Diwali box.
"I'll count them out. One for you, one for me, one for Ma, one for Papa..."
"That's slow. Do it in your head."
"Twelve divided by four... three! Three each."
"Right. Now Ma says she only wants half of hers, and we can share the rest."
Damini frowned. "Half of three is one and a half. So one and a half left over, split between two of us..."
She counted on her fingers, then grinned. "We each get three and three-quarters!"
Tarun blinked. "I hadn't even worked that out yet."

qa.q: How many kaju barfis were in the Diwali box?
qa.a: There were twelve kaju barfis.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Tarun says the answer hadn't been worked out yet?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and pleased that her fraction answer came first. 😊

qa.q: How could a parent build on Damini's sweet-box maths?
qa.a: They could use more real-life sharing, like cutting a roti into quarters, and let her explain her steps.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun when Damini solves it first?
qa.a: Tarun is surprised and probably impressed, having set the puzzle without finishing it.

grounding: Shows a child moving beyond counting to division and fractions while sharing festival sweets.

passage:
"Okay, Rafiq, listen to all four steps before you touch anything," said Manoj, spreading kite paper on the terrace two days before Uttarayan.
"First, fold the paper corner to corner. Second, glue the long stick down the fold. Third, bend the thin stick across and tie it. Fourth, trim the extra paper."
"Got it."
"Say them back."
"Fold, glue the long stick, bend and tie the thin one... and cut the extra."
"Good. Last year you forgot after step one."
Rafiq worked slowly, whispering, "Third... tie it." His kite came out a little crooked, but it held.
"Will it fly?"
"Tomorrow we test it," said Manoj.

qa.q: How many steps did Manoj explain?
qa.a: Manoj explained four steps.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq whisper "Third... tie it" while working?
qa.a: He was concentrating hard to keep the steps in mind, determined not to lose track this year.

qa.q: What part of Manoj's teaching helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking Rafiq to say the steps back helped him hold all four in memory before starting.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel seeing Rafiq finish the kite?
qa.a: Manoj would likely feel pleased and proud, remembering that Rafiq forgot after step one only last year.

grounding: Illustrates a child's growing working memory as he holds and follows a four-step kite-making instruction.
